utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the parties may have some preliminaries. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Just briefly. Yesterday I mentioned a Rule 70 document which we had not had clearance to disclose. Late last evening we did receive an e-mail giving us permission. The official correspondence hasn't come, but on that basis we are authorised to disclose it. We've done that. We will have printed copies made prior to it being uploaded into e-court should Defence counsel wish to use it with the witness. The only thing that remains, Your Honour, the Prosecution would request the Chamber to instruct the witness. The witness had been told that there was no permission yet to discuss this document. But would the Chamber please advise the witness that the document that he was told not to mention that clearance has been given and if asked questions about it, he is free to answer. And one qualification, that the right to use and permission to use it is condition that it be done in private session. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Groome. If I address the witness in relation to this, perhaps I could do that best in private session anyhow. That would be better. Any preliminaries from the Defence or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We had slight miscommunication with the Detention Unit this morning. There are some medical doctors who were scheduled to examine Mr. Mladic, and we ask the Detention Unit not to send him to the court this morning, but, unfortunately, there was probably some miscommunication and Mr. Mladic is with us this morning. And we would ask Your Honours kindly to ask Mr. Mladic to give his waiver and leave the courtroom as soon as possible so that the doctors can continue their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you can take instructions on behalf of Mr. Mladic, and if he wishes to waive his right, you can [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, please, if you consult with Mr. Mladic make clear that, of course, he is entitled to attend the hearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have a clear instruction from Mr. Mladic that he is waiving his right to be present today and tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Mladic can be escorted out of the courtroom. I do not know how quickly transportation to the UNDU can be organised because that is in the hands of Registry together with the transport services of the Dutch authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I will also kindly ask your permission to leave the courtroom because I have to organise a visit again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic is still there as co-counsel. Well, further conversations can be done outside of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser, are you ready to continue your examination? I will ask that the witness could be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we're ready to proceed. Actually, as the witness is being brought in, if I could ask -- I'd like to start with P429 on the -- up on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mole. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'd like to move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Hochhauser will now continue her examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Mole.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: We left off yesterday discussing the difference between an observation post and a weapons monitoring site and I think we sort of stopped mid-answer due to a translation problem. So can you tell us just briefly what is an observation post?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: An observation post was utilised so that we could gather information throughout the Sarajevo area, but it was very specifically orientated towards the Papa side. As I was explaining yesterday, there were less weapons for us to monitor in -- on Papa side, and, as a consequence, we had manpower available for us to use within the city, to observe the city, rather than to monitor the weapons, and I think, as I mentioned yesterday, the weapon monitoring was mostly occurring on the Lima side. So we set up a number of observe posts which actually had been arranged before I came to Sarajevo, and I adjusted some of them during the course of my tour, but the aim was for those observation posts to be on high ground, which, necessarily, placed them quite close to the front line so that they could observe the whole of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, if we could view for a moment, please, Exhibit P429, which is referenced in paragraph 14 of your statement. Now, the -- the triangle -- sorry, is it up on your screen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a map on the screen if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. And the triangles that we see up on this map which are designated with either an L and a number or a P and a number, do those reflect only the observation posts or also the weapons monitoring sites?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's both.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And does this actually reflect where those were located during your time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now yesterday we discussed the standardised form used to collect the information from both of those types of sites. If we could look for a moment, please, at Exhibit P427. And do you see that on your monitor now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. P427 is marked on the top, designated on top as an increp from the 3rd December 1992, and is this an example of the standardised form that you were discussing in your statement and yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, if you could just briefly illustrate for the Chamber what information you were recording and how by going through the columns. And so I'm going to ask you first, this P5/1 in the first column on the left of the document, labelled serial what is that -- what -- what information is recorded there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: P5 relates to where the observation was taken from, in this case observation point Papa 5. The slash follows and then the incident number is indicated by the next number.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And just with again with reference to the prior exhibit that we saw, P429, Papa 5 would have been designated on that map with a triangle P5?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, I think the date is the self-explanatory and the time. Can you tell us what is recorded in activity details?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be as much detail as the observer could place that relates to the type of weapon that was presumed to have fired, where it landed and any other detail, numerics, i.e., how many rounds landed in that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And so, for an example, just -- if we can take this -- staying with the first entry could you interpret what is said -- what is recorded for us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do my best but bearing in mind it was other people's hieroglyphics, not mine. But I would guess that's artillery rounds for IRTY; MR would be mortar rounds; AAA would be anti-aircraft weapon; and 5, I think that's got a squiggle there that says "tank." So that would be five tank rounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And you said you are deciphering other people's hieroglyphics. Back when you were in Sarajevo, were you looking at these reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They would interpret those in a much more co-ordinated fashion when they were sent through to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: But is this an example of the -- of the type of form on which they were recording them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the base document that recording was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now - thank you - moving over to the remarks column -- I'm sorry to the source of information column, which is the next column. Can you tell us what that records?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, para 5 would be the source or the presumed source of the incident which occurred in the previous paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've used the word -- you just used the word "presumed" and I think in your previous answer you also used the word "presumed" in describing the presumed type of artillery or type of weaponry. Can you tell us was there a standard that was dictated by you to the UNMOs that had to be met before they would record something on a form like this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The court reporters asks for short breaks between question and answer an answer and question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you just ask that question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm sorry, I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Before one of your UN MOs would -- would record a round, can you tell us was there a protocol for what -- what standard of information they had to have in order to record it as a round observed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All UNMOs when they came into our sector were introduced to these forms and instructed on how to fill them out, so that was a universal training element for all UNMOs whether they be Lima or Papa side. Part of that training would have been what you've just asked. They had to see the impact of the round, and then they had to make an assessment as to what the round was from what weapon it came, and, if possible, give an indication of where that round came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And so when it says UNMO seen, is that an indication that the recording UNMO actually observed the round landing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And in remarks where it says area Otes or Ilidza is that where -- what is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the area from -- of the source of the rounds which they've observed and the figures after that would be the four-figure grid reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And can we see briefly the second page of this document, please. And can you explain to the Court what it is that we're looking at here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we see here is the obverse of the form that you've just been looking at. The particular date of that particular form was during the Otes conflict, which you see Otes mentioned a number of times on the form, on both sides. But the conflict was so intense that quite clearly the form was not fit for purpose, and so they had to turn over and continue the recording. So what you see are groups of five rounds and then the totals at the end of each.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you had an opportunity to review the Senior Military Observer's end-of-month of reports for October, November, and December 1992, which are now in evidence respectively as Exhibits P424, 425, and 426. In addition to the information recorded on forms such as the one that's on the monitor, can you tell the Chamber, were there other sources of information that you used in compiling these end -- the end-of-month reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The end-of-month report was an assimilation of a considerable amount of detail which came to us from multiple sources. Before I went to Sarajevo, I was fortunately exposed to a number of different areas within the theatre, and hopefully after this brief explanation it will make sense to answer your question. But I was in the UN protected area east operating from Erdut. I was the chief operations officer for all of the UNMO group. That allowed me to take information from reports such as you're asking me about from the Senior Military Observers in all UN protected areas and to assimilate and interpret them. I visited all the UN protected areas and, as well as that, I went to Bihac. After that was when I was posted to Sarajevo, and as a consequence I feel that I was well rounded in the information available to me within the theatre. Now I've explained that, you'll see that the end-of-month report that I was submitting was just but one of a sequence of reports that would come from all UN protected areas. And it was a two-way process. So once that information went to Zagreb to the Chief Military Observer, a co-ordinated report was then sent back out to all the Senior Military Observers as to what was going on elsewhere in theatre. There were other agencies within Sarajevo. The Red Cross weren't there for very long. UNHCR, three battalions, of course, of UNPROFOR. And, primarily, my operations room was adjacent to and worked closely with the operations room belonging to the sector headquarters with whom I worked. They, too, had sources of information which came from multiple agencies. Where did we share this information? We shared it daily at an O Group operations meeting in the morning. There may be one in the afternoon when all elements of UNPROFOR at the PTT building came together, shared their knowledge, and looked to the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I'm going to diverge from the route I was on for a moment and ask you as a follow-up to that question or that answer did you, all of the sources of information that you've just told us about and the sharing of information, were you able -- did you use that information in order to analyse and -- analyse what was happening in Sarajevo and determine what your next steps would be there, and, if so, can you tell us what the result of that was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. The point of sharing the information was to give myself and my UNMOs the best opportunity to achieve the tasks which I was setting them or which I was set by the Chief Military Observer or, indeed, the Sector Commander. So I needed to interpret events throughout the theatre, to see if they were going to have any direct effect on Sarajevo as a sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "throughout the theatre," can you define what your -- what that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The theatre, to me, would be all the UN protected areas both on the edge of Bosnia, within Bosnia, Bihac, all UN protected areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And did you find -- did you find that events throughout all of the other protected areas had a direct effect on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Part of my analysis was a military one. I applied what knowledge I had from 24 years service in my military to interpret what was going on around me to people who haven't experienced such as a siege of a city. It all looks somewhat chaotic. But there was structure there, and it was that structure I was trying to interpret using the data which we're talking about. So, for example, when I was not in Sarajevo but the Chief Operations Officer, I was aware of the pressure point of Brcko. It was significant for both sides, and I won't go into the detail about that, other than to say that if a threat to such a sensitive area of Bosnia was perceived by, for example, the Serb side throughout the theatre, there was often a retaliation, or we would expect a retaliation in Sarajevo. And it was not accidental because my other experience of having relationships with Colonel Galic, later General Galic, was such that I had been told that there will be responses in Sarajevo should things not go according to their plans elsewhere within the theatre. So there was a marked relationship between events in the theatre and those that we experienced in the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And Colonel you discuss this somewhat also in your statement. And in your statement at paragraphs 35 to 36 you say that: "The Serbs risked more by trying to take Sarajevo militarily than the possible advantages gained by doing so. The position they were already in allowed them to achieve their political aims. They could do this by applying pressure to the city to achieve their aims elsewhere." When you say "applying pressure," in that context, what is it that you observed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, the city, as you will be aware, was in a siege condition. The front line was about 65 kilometres right round the city, so militarily it was encircled. And in my statements I have expressed that the Serb side were weapons-heavy, i.e., they had heavy weapons and they were light on artillery -- on infantry, I'm sorry. The best way for them to respond - bearing in mind that to attempt to take any part of a city in an urban conflict is an infantry-orientated operation, and I've just said to you that they were not very strong with infantry - would be to respond with their heavy weapons. That, we noticed, by virtue of the increased activity of increps, which we've discussed already, within the city, as a result, and after events elsewhere within the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And so, when you say -- thank you. When you say: "As a result and after events elsewhere within the theatre -- within the theatre," are you talking about fire into the city that was not responsive to any fire at Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That begs another question which is to determine whether any particular round or any particular fire mission had a military objective or not. I've explained the surrounding front line round the city, and you would expect military activity within that zone. You would expect that with heavy weapons, the Serbs on Lima side would have the opportunity and the capability to target military objectives within the city. If you do that as a commander of artillery pieces, accepting it's an indirect fire weapon, it's an area weapon, it's not hugely accurate, but you can lay down a fire mission which is concentrated. And that would be the natural response to a military target. So, when you look at the shelling in Sarajevo, we then need to decide what all the other rounds were that were impacting on the city. It is that element, the element which it is difficult to determine that there was a military target which had preempted that action that we would call indiscriminate. Because we know that the Serb side had the capability of creating an effective fire mission on a very concentrated part of the city because the exhibit that's still up in front of me of Papa 5, the increp, indicates exactly that: An effective fire mission from a number of weapon sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm going to interrupt you there for a second. First of all, can you tell us what -- what is the definition that you're using for "fire mission," and then after that can you also -- can you tell us how you know that they were capable of doing it, an effective fire mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document we see in front of us are the effects of a fire missions, but if you go to the other end, and that is, say, the weapons site, the gun placement, the commander would be given instructions as to what target he had, how many rounds he would be expected to support his commander with, and he would have a range map, and he would know precisely what his target was. He would make up his own fire plan from the request from his commander. And bearing in mind his own capability and the range of his weapon and the amount of ammunition he has, he would make his plan up based on that information that he had been given and instructed to execute. Does that answer the question on the fire plan?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I think it answers the question on the fire mission. When you said that you could see from the increp that's still on the screen that -- that the Serb forces around Sarajevo were capable of doing an effective fire mission, targeted mission, can you tell us what is it that's in this increp that tells you that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've got a mixture of weapons which were annotated in the incidents on the other side of this piece of paper, which indicates that the rounds came from a number of different weapon sites, but they all impacted in the same place. So that shows the effectiveness of a fire plan co-ordinated beyond the weapon sites, up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 22 of your amalgamated statement of P421, you describe how you encouraged the UNMOs under your command to develop a relationship with the local commanders. And you conclude that paragraph by noting: "Sometimes the mere fact that they would ask what the battery commander was doing would result in a reduced level of engagement." Can you explain what you mean by that, in light of what we've just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to extricate my response here from what we were talking about, because where specifically we're talking about a fire mission, that required co-ordination and instruction from up the chain of command. That element of the statement which you've just read out was directed more at the following situation. The UN Military Observers on Lima side were on gun-sites, and the gun-sites were not always employed in fire missions; but every now and again, the weapons would be fired. So it would be irrelevant and unseemly for an UN Military Observer, in a well-organised fire mission, to approach the commander of the weapons. And he would know that. He would be appreciative of the fact that it was part of a larger operation. But if just his weapon site was being employed and rounds were fired from the weapons that he was monitoring, he would talk to the gun commanders. He would ask to see the range map. He would ask what the targets were, the perceived targets were, where that information had come from, and what they were intending to achieve by firing their weapons. You can imagine that if anybody from this court just walked up to talk to a local commander and ask him those questions without a relationship he would probably be marched off the site. The point was the UN Military Observers had built up a sort of relationship with these commanders. In my statements from before, I explained that I tried to stop a frequent movement of UN Military Observers on rotation because it broke that important link with local commanders. Does that answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Well, what I'd like to know is -- what I'd like to know is focussing on this -- the latter part of the statement, when it -- when you say that fostering these relations resulted in a reduced level of engagement, and so I'd like to know if can you explain to the Chamber how is that that it resulted in a reduced level of engagement? What was it that your UNMOs were finding when they engaged with these commanders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effect of that relationship and the effect of the discussion which you would engage in as a UN Military Observer on a weapons site would be to elicit the information which I have already described. Now, sometimes some of the answers that were received were not particularly militarily orientated, and I have in my statements before expressed my personal experience on a gun-site when I've asked why the weapons were being fired, and on one occasion at a mortar site I was instructed that the barrels were being warmed --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry. I'm just going to interrupt you for one second again, because the Chamber is in possession of your statement, and so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I see whether I can cut this short. Let me first see whether I understood your question well and then to see whether from what you told us, Mr. Mole, whether I understood, more or less, your position. Was it the case that when there was intense firing, or whatever, that because your observers knew meanwhile those on the firing positions that they would say, Hey, what are you doing? And that, as a result of that, that the intensity of the fire or the direction of the fire would be less. Is that more or less what you wanted to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be affected that way but there are conditions to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but just -- I think you were trying to find out, Ms. Hochhauser, what the gist of the answer was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. And I was also just going to point the Chamber, I think, to paragraph 80 of the witness's statement in which I think that you write about the story that you were -- it contains the story I think you were just going to tell us about the warming of the barrels. So we can move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it was conditioned, Mr. Mole. If you can explain that in one or two lines, you're invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If -- do you want to explain it in one or two lines or ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think from what I've heard that the statement covers it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. So I'm now going to move on to a different document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 2353 on the monitor. And specifically starting at e-court page 9 in the English, which I believe is the middle of e-court page 13 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you had the opportunity to read the statement of Radovan Karadzic regarding the fifth strategic objective which begins in the last two sentences of e-court page 9 in the English and continues through the end of the first full paragraph on e-court page 10 prior to coming to court today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And I'll ask if -- once we've had the opportunity to read those last two sentences, if we can just move to page 10 in the English. Once you've had an opportunity to review it again, just let me know and I'll ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, at paragraphs 35 to 36 of your statement, you discuss what you labelled as a policy of containment in Sarajevo and what you observed about that policy of containment during your time there. In light of that, I'd like to ask for your comment on the portion of 65 ter 2353 in which Radovan Karadzic says: "In addition, the fighting in Sarajevo keeps the fighting away from the Krajina far from the Semberija, far from the Drina, far away from all those areas where we could possibly have conflicts with Muslims." I'd like to ask for your comment based on your own observations and experience in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statements about the containment of Sarajevo were originally formalised by understanding the military situations within the city and around it in my first two months there. I've already indicated that events elsewhere in Bosnia would have an effect on Sarajevo. I had never seen this document before, but it is really interesting that I had come to the conclusions that I had and to see it confirmed like this - I think this is an assembly document - was, to me, quite a revelation and fitted in with what I've already described to you by virtue of travelling around the UN protected areas. The major impact of the war had left those UN protected areas and were now concentrated around Sarajevo. So this document confirmed everything that I had determined for myself by the various sources I described and my experience in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Mole, did you ever encounter Mr. Mladic during your time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had imposed upon us an organisation called the mixed military working group. It meet frequently from, I think, the 5th of November, 1992, was the first one that I recall, and it met frequently but not regularly for the next two months. It would be within that meeting that I met General Mladic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And just briefly, the purpose of those mixed military working groups was what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I explain that we had a sector headquarters within Bosnia, but we also had the second-in-command of UNPROFOR was General Morillon, and he was tasked with setting up BiH command, i.e., UNPROFOR command not in Zagreb but nearby in Kiseljak near Sarajevo. It was that headquarters's initiative to have a mixed military working group, the idea being to bring together the various elements, the combative elements, at a meeting to try and negotiate a cease-fire and a demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And are you able to tell the Chamber precisely when or how many times Mr. Mladic attended that meeting while you were also there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall him being there a number of times. I recall we had lunches, but I wouldn't put dates on those events. But I did note that I had in a previous statement mentioned that I had taken a message from General Morillon and handed it to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And do you -- if you're able to, do you recall when -- when Mr. Mladic would attend those meetings, would he be the sole representative of the VRS there or would Galic be with him or -- if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That element changed significantly with each meeting. We set up a -- a working group where the principals were not present but staff officers were, or within the aegis of the mixed military working group. So sometimes he would be there. Sometimes General Gvero would be there representing that side. Sometimes Galic would be there. And it was a very variable feast. Sometimes, of course, some people couldn't get there by virtue of military activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 58 of your statement which is page 14 in e-court you state that the SRK's ability, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps's ability to communicate with elements outside the corps which you observed indicated that the corps itself was under command. Drawing your attention to that statement I would like to ask you if you made any such observations about the command structure over the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited the operations room in the barracks with General Galic and was able to view that and saw all the components that I would expect of a headquarters which allowed communication, both to subunits and elsewhere, within the theatre. Did what General Galic do and what happened around Sarajevo with the Romanija Corps, was it affected by what went on elsewhere? Well, it must do. I'm going to have to ask you now precisely what the question is, because, otherwise, depends where I'm going with the explanation. Are you saying -- are you asking me, did I physically see or do something to make me understand that there was -- the Romanija Corps was under command.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Well, what I'm asking is: Based on your own personal observations based on anything General Galic or anybody else in that command said to you, and also your observations of how the command was operating.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Understood. So I've already described how I saw Sarajevo and the Romanija Corps operating within the context of the theatre of Bosnia, and it was obvious to me that there would be limitations and, indeed, instructions passed to General Galic as to how he would achieve his objective because he wasn't working alone. We know that because I've already described that events elsewhere in Bosnia impacted seriously upon the city, and that sort of information flow had to come from somewhere else, and it's natural it would come through the chain of command. But from my own personal experience as a logistician what ammunition, manpower, weapons, and so on, were allocated to the task for Sarajevo for the Romanija Corps would be just part of what the overall operation was and cannot be separated from the overall operation within Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would now be the right time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me say something about these breaks. We have these short sessions and short breaks mainly because that was the wish of Mr. Mladic. Therefore we either could take the break now and follow the usual schedule. We also could continue for a while. But I'm also addressing the witness. Mr. Mole, it may be that you prefer to have a break now. Then we'll take that break as well. But if at any other point in time you would think it would be better for you to have a break, don't hesitate to address me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I have no preference, Your Honour. It is entirely up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no preference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're at Your Honours' pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I suggest that we follow the usual procedure and take the break now and stick to the short breaks. We'll take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Ms. Hochhauser, as far as time is concerned, your estimate was one hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It has become clear I think that I will need a little more time than that. I don't think that will affect our schedule for the week since we're down a witness. I hope to be done in 15 minutes. I hope to use an additional 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we are at this moment at one hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Right, so 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, so then I expect you -- yes, perhaps the more focussed your questions are, the more focused answers you can expect. And if the witness nevertheless delves in various directions, it's up to you to get him back on the right track.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, Ms. Hochhauser will now continue her examination. May I invite you to focus very much on the very precise answers [sic] she'll ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll do my best, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: In your last answer, Colonel Mole, you began to talk about logistics, such as ammunition and manpower, weapons. And I would ask you to please to take a look if we could have 65 ter 28456.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Although, actually, it comes to mind, Your Honours, that we've now come to the first of the two documents which the Prosecution in its motion sought to -- sought leave to add to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So I raise that with you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, any specific objections on this specific document? I mean, not the -- what you have already submitted in writing, but any specifics on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think apart from what we've submitted in writing, we don't have anything further to say as to this specific document. At this point in time, we'll see what the answers to the questions that are asked and if the witness is appropriate for entering this document into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll -- adding to the 65 ter list is not -- is -- consent is given by the Chamber. Let's then hear what questions you have and whether it causes any problems to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So, Colonel, looking at 65 ter 28456, this is a 26 November order for further activities, signed by Stanislav Galic. You had the opportunity to review this document before today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And does this document also address the time-period of the Otes offensive that you have been telling us about or you touched upon in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it just precedes that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, does this document comport with the activities of the RSK -- SRK - excuse me - that you observed during the time that you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document I think explains what we knew as Operation Envelope which was a response by the Serb side to military activities on the Presidency side.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And can you -- turning to paragraph 13 which is in e-court page -- sorry. Have I written it here as 23. Is that -- could that be correct? Yes, and I apologise to counsel. I actually did not note the B/C/S page, corresponding page, entitled -- words logistical support. Can you relate what is in that portion of the document about logistical support to what you were just telling us about logistics in your own observations of the SRK and control over the SRK in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first saw this document, it linked well with my understanding of logistics, being that I was a logistics officer. Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was but part of the army command in Bosnia on the Serb side. So any army commander would obviously have limitations to his theatre of operations, based on available manpower, weapons, and ammunition, primarily. As I say, Romanija Corps was just part of the overall army command, so the balance of how much logistics support was given to Romanija Corps in relation to other units competing for finite resources within the military in Bosnia, this document accords to that process.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And specifically in terms of what you observed at the functioning of the Romanija Corps while you were there can you tell us what your -- what your thoughts are about this 50 per cent expenditure rate that we see there for ammunition.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It indicates that the local commander has operational freedom for 50 per cent of the held ammunition, for example. And, therefore, he has considerable latitude to do with that as he will. But principally here, the other 50 per cent is not within the local commander's gift.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And the operational freedom is that given from -- given from whom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be given from the army headquarters, staff officers, I assume, working on behalf of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, at -- excuse me, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, I would just ask to mark this for identification at this point, this document. I don't want ask to tender it given the length of the document and the small portion of which the witness has commented on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you want then to later -- is it because you have not quoted any part of it. You just -- I mean, for those who read the transcript later, it will be unclear exactly what the document said, which the witness had looked at before.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sorry, let me clear that up. The document that we are referring to is the 26 November order for further activities signed by Stanislav --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's not the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's about content. I mean, you asked the witness to comment on something without the portion having been read and if you don't tender it then there will be a big puzzle for those who later read the transcript. Now, what is your intention not to tender it at all? That would create this problem. Or do you intend to tender at a later stage a smaller portion of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'll actually tender the whole document at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I believe that the parts that the witness has testified about rightly do become part of the record. I don't actually even know what's in the entirety of the 23 pages here, but I don't think that the witness can authenticate or provide us with the information on that so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have it marked for identification and the parties are invited to sit together to see what is the relevant portion, and if at any other point in time we would need the entire document then, of course, the parties could exchange views on that and see whether there would be an objection at this moment to have the whole of the document admitted into evidence --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The importance of that would be that we do not have one document page 7, three lines here in evidence, page 10 somewhere else in evidence. So if you could sit together and see whether you could reach agreement on what and how we should admit this document into evidence. It will be marked for identification. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28456 will receive number P430, MFI'd, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you have not yet tendered the previous document which that was 02353. That was the session -- and that's also a very long document so I also wonder how to deal with that document. But you used only a very small portion of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I would -- I would tender that document as well. We can, of course, handle that will the same way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it will be marked for identification for the time being. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2353 becomes Exhibit P431, MFI'd, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber hear from the parties not later than tomorrow close of business.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, and also to just address the hole in the record that Your Honour correctly pointed out to me, in case the document doesn't come in, I would like to read the first paragraph of the -- that I was referring to that I asked the witness about, which is under logistic support. I had referred the witness to the paragraph that reads: "The approved ammunition expenditure and fuel consumption per unit is a maximum of 50 per cent of the quantity originally found in the units. The units must make sure that the remaining 50 per cent is not spent and will be kept solely as precious reserve."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at least the portion you have drawn the attention of the witness to is now on the record. Yes, Ms. Hochhauser, you said you would like to do that and instead of waiting for the Chamber to do say --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that this is the appropriate way of proceeding, you did it --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- just as before when you said, I need another 15 minutes. You didn't ask for another 15 minutes but you said you needed another 15 minutes. I will not make a drama out of it, but that's good manners in the courtroom. Then it has been read into the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter 11354 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And this is the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps document number 10/74695 a regular combat report signed by Stanislav Galic, dated the 2nd December 1992. And, sir, have you had an opportunity to look at this document prior to coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And again, does this document reflect what you observed at that time in Sarajevo and particularly in the advancement of the Otes offensive as of the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see down to paragraph 4, and that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Perhaps if -- thank you. We can see the whole document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, sir, can you comment on this document in terms of the logistics and command and control observations that we've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation on Otes would not be one that was decided upon by a local commander because, as I've already suggested, resources were limited throughout theatre and the army commander would obviously allocate resources where he wanted them to be allocated. So the operation was done under the instruction of the army command.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, the army command at what level?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the army, General Mladic, I would assume, would sanction the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And in terms of logistics, is there anything remarkable to you even in the sentence that refers to the winter gear provided?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It links back to what I was referring to shortly a few moments ago, relating to ammunition, trained manpower, weapons, and it includes, obviously, rations, winter gear, and they would be a theatre resource. They wouldn't be a resource which an individual commander could necessarily deal with. He would be making requests upon the army command for those items.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might I'd like to tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 11354 becomes Exhibit P432, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And, Your Honours, we come to the second of the two documents that were subject of the motion to add, which is 65 ter -- what we've assigned, pending your permission, 65 ter 28457.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Leave is granted to add it to your 65 ter list. We'll decide on admission once we've dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And if we could see that document, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, this is a document dated 4 December 1992, also from the SRK command. And I have the same question for you as to this document that I had for the previous two, which is: Can you comment on it in terms whether it comports with what you saw during that time in Sarajevo, as well as with what you observed the command and control with regard to the SRK? And, I'm sorry, and specifically with logistics.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 is clearly a demand for combat rations. The army land forces are being requested. And it supports what I said a few moments ago, that requests for logistical support are coming through the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further specifics, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28457 becomes Exhibit P433, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, sir, Colonel, if you can tell us also of your observations and interactions with the individual commanders on the ground in Sarajevo during the time you were there. Did you see that they were, in fact, supplied by the command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In previous statements, I have indicated that I saw resupply on many of the gun-sites on Lima side. I mentioned that I had seen stockpiles of ammunition at the weapon sites. I connect that to the operation at Otes that we've been discussing, and the demands upon, for example, ammunition would have been intense and would have had to have been requested through the chain of command and certainly was not available to the local commander throughout the remainder of my tour that I saw; i.e., the stocks I saw on a day-to-day basis would have to be enhanced significantly for a fire mission that we watched unfold during the course of the Otes conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, sir, we keep referring back to the Otes conflict I think as an example of an effective fire mission, but the concepts that we've been talking about are applicable also -- are they applicable also during the time-period that there wasn't such a mission occurring in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The extraordinary extreme of the Otes one is what captures our attention, but, of course, what one might term as standard resupply happened continually throughout the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser, you earlier indicated 15 to 20 minutes. We're at now more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. With the Court's permission, I have one last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put that last question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. Which is about Exhibit P425. If we could see that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, as it's coming up, I just -- I have a question about this Senior Military Observer's end-of-month report. The one we're looking at is for December but consistently through the end-of-month reports we see that in the daily entries there are discrepancies between the number of rounds recorded as outgoing from a particular side and the number of corresponding rounds recorded as incoming from the other side. And I just -- if you can give us, please, a brief explanation as to what factored into those discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't monitor all the weapons within the range of Sarajevo, only those that were selectively given to us as a result of the airport agreement. So consequently weapons were brought into the theatre -- into the area and used and moved away and there were others that were static in the location but we still didn't monitor those, nor did he have UN Military Observers sufficient to do so. And then there is the fall of shot, i.e., not always do we know what the target is of the weapons that we're not monitoring and we don't know where that fall of shot is. So, yes, there was a discrepancy between the two sets of figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hochhauser. Mr. Ivetic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Mladic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Colonel. I'd like to remind you that since we do speak the same language we have to try and ensure a pause between question and answer so as to assist the interpreters and the court reporter in doing their tasks today.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, prior to your deployment to Sarajevo as SMO on 16 September 1992, did you have occasion to receive any instruction or training relative to the military structure or operative rules of either the JNA, the VRS, or the Army of BiH?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll appreciate that it was early in the conflict and the knowledge base for the question you've just asked wasn't good. There was some instruction, but, to be fair, you would have to find out for yourself on your deployment the answer to some of the questions, quite a lot of the questions, that you pose.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. And you yourself personally had no prior familiarity with either the SFRY or its armed forces; that is to say, you had not studied them as part of your formal education or your military education; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had studied the eastern bloc so there was a significance there relating to weaponry but, of course, each country organises themselves totally differently. And since we were talking about the origin of three components which were new on the world stage, your statement is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to clear up something that you just discussed. For that purpose, I would ask for Exhibit P430 to be called up on e-court. And if we could focus on the first page for the moment and we'll wait for the English to come up. Sir, I would direct your attention to the -- to the sender of the document which is reflected in the upper left corner. Would you agree with me that this is, in fact, an order sent by the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you recall, this is the document that has - I believe, page 23 in e-court in the English. I'm not sure of the B/C/S page - but has the selection giving what you said was operational freedom over 50 per cent of the stocks of munitions, and I believe that you had identified this as coming from the -- from the Main Staff. Would you agree that if this is an order from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, it would be Commander Galic giving this freedom to his subordinates rather than the Main Staff giving this freedom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within my many statements that I've made in evidence in these courts, I have explained in some detail the equivalent logistic expressions that we used in the British Army, and it's a unit called the daily ammunition expenditure rete. That was an indicator, a planning guide that was imposed upon you as a commander to indicate how much you could hold, how much you would use on a daily basis. You would exceed that if you went into an operation which you were commanded to do. And you would be allocated, maybe, one, two, or more, DAERs to fulfil that obligation. It matters not that this was an instruction downwards in the chain of command. What it indicates is that there is one that is throughout the chain of command. It would be pointless. He was expressing that 50 per cent which is close to a DAER if he wasn't having one imposed upon him. So it's an indicator that there is a chain of command and that this is part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Would you agree with me that the UNMO mission was not there on the ground to count shells in and out; that is to say, it was not within the remit of the UNMO group to investigate all rounds that were fired, impact areas, nor to assess the rights or wrongs of the conflict on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment, please, and I'll read that question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. What the UNMO mission was there to facilitate, amongst many other aspects, was to find a level of truth as to what was happening so that interpretation of that could be then briefed to the world through the United Nations and the secretariat. So to identify our tasks specifically just to count rounds in and out, is to be extremely simplistic. We were determining the events and interpreting them, and it was a neutral observation as opposed to taking the word of the combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you would allow me to go back to the previous question because I do not know for sure whether I understood your answer. That was about the chain of command and General Galic giving orders downwards. Did I understand your answer well that you would say it would be pointless to impose such a 50 per cent rule, if I could say so, if not, a similar thing happened in the chain of command above you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then I have understood your rather lengthy answer but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but some of them are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can follow up on the question that I had asked and the answer that the Colonel had received, if we can call up 1D390 in e-court and it will be the 11th page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the transcript of your testimony from the Karadzic proceedings, and the selection that I'm calling up is transcript page 5890, 12 to 18, and it was the bases for my question. I'd like to focus on lines 12 through 18 of that transcript. And there, as I understood your answer to the question that was posed by

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC'S TIME WAS
utterances.text: "The UNMO mission was not there to count shells in and out. It was there to assess situations, provide humanitarian support, and the other tasks that I've already outlined, part of which would be observing the conflict as it developed. It was not within the remit of the UNMO group to investigate all rounds that were fired, impact areas, and so on, nor was it the UNMO's task to assess the rights or wrongs of conflict on the front line." Sir, do you recall this testimony that you gave in the Karadzic proceedings, and do you stand by it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It expresses exactly what I am still trying to explain. It is too simplistic to assume that because we're counting shells in and out that we're not doing anything with that information. And that paragraph slightly out of context was an attempt to resolve that disconnect. It wasn't sufficient just to count the rounds in and out. What we were attempting to do was to, as I have explained in that paragraph, interpret it, not assess the rights and wrongs, but give impressions from what -- our observations to the world as to what was going on in Sarajevo. Part of that was to watch what rounds were fired by whom, where, so that we could better answer observations made by the combatants who would make complaint to the UN about what had happened, and we would have a neutral source from whence we could make our decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in so far as it was not within the remit of the UNMO mission to assess right or wrong, that any assessments that may be considered to do that within your testimony or your statement, that is to say, qualify a shelling as either legitimate or wrongful, must be considered with regard to that caveat that such conclusions were beyond the remit of the UNMO mission that you were there to perform?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I object to that question. I don't think that -- I don't think -- I think that it's a mixing of terms in terms of right and wrong from one piece of prior testimony and legitimacy and not legitimacy. I think it is phrased in a little bit of an unfair way to the witness and I would ask that it be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And one of the problems with the previous quote you gave, lines 12 to 18, is that you have not drawn the attention of witness and our attention to the question which preceded that answer. It's impossible, I think, to understand that question without looking at a question, which amounts more to a speech than to a question in which is found in the lines 2 to 9. But please rephrase your question and proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree that any assessments that may be considered as expressing an opinion that artillery fire was right or wrong from your testimony or your statement must be considered with this caveat that this would be -- such determination were beyond the remit of the UNMO mission that you were in Sarajevo to perform?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have rephrased it but the substance is exactly the same. Could you please rephrase it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe, Your Honours, the objection was for me mixing the words right and wrong with legitimate and unlegitimate. So I'm using the exact same words that the witness used in his answer in the Karadzic proceedings. I don't know how other to rephrase it without going away from the testimony of the witness that he just affirmed that it was beyond the remit of the UNMO mission to assess right or wrong. And I'm simply asking whether that is something that should be considered in conjunction with any conclusions in his witness statement or his testimony where he attempts to assert right or wrong to actions of artillery attack or fire mission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I help here, sir? I'm quite happy to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although it's not a common way of proceeding, but if you can assist the parties and the Chamber, it might help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The statement on the screen is rights or wrongs of conflict on the front line. You are co-joining that expression with whether rounds were targeted or whether they were not. The two are totally separate. When I say the rights and wrongs of the conflict on the front line, I'm not evaluating whether somebody is or isn't right, to react or act in a certain way. But when it comes to rounds landing within an area, we were trying to determine whether they were targeted against military targets, or whether they were not. That is not the same as right and wrong on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Here you also say that it was not within the remit of the UNMO group to investigate all rounds that were fired and impact areas. Would you also agree that you did not have access to any of the target grids or maps or other intel being used by either side to direct their fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I take the first part of your question, where you say: Here you also say that it was not within the remit of the UNMO group to investigate all rounds that were fired at impact areas. Now, that is correct. Because one would only investigate in detail if there was an incident of one or two rounds in a day, but we were in a war zone. You have seen from my testimony before what a quiet day, what a normal day and what a busy day was and the number of impacts in the city. So to forensically determine the detail you've just described for all that military activity, I'm not saying it wasn't within our remit. It was not possible to do that. Because you're assuming that we would go to an impact and investigate it in a forensic military police fashion. That definitely was not within our remit. As to the second part of your question that relates to target grids or maps, I'm sorry to say that you're wrong there. I visited the operations rooms of both sides, and in previous testimonies, I have stated that. I asked both sides what they thought the other side was doing to obtain the information that I required. I've also described to you that UNMOs definitely did look at range maps on the gun-sites that they were monitoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did any of the range maps that you saw have any improper targets that would not be considered legitimate military targets on them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just stated that UN Military Observers would look at range maps which were those being used by weapons site commanders. I wasn't a weapons site commander, nor was I an UNMO on a weapons site.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at paragraph 72 of your amalgamated statement, which is P421. And this will be page 17 in the English, page 18 in the B/C/S. And here, as we wait for it, the -- should be the prior page. There we go. And here, sir, you describe efforts to try and identify military installations to try and rationalise your observations and to corroborate or dispute justifications the Serbs provided. You indicate that it was never within the mandate of the UNMO mission to maintain a list of, quote/unquote, "military targets on either side." Would you agree with me that even apart from the mandate, the very ability of the UNMO mission to identify or list military targets was severely limited due to several factors, including the limited personnel and the war conditions in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not totally sure of your question. Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. Would you agree with me that even apart from the lack of a mandate, the very ability of the UNMO mission to identify or list military targets was limited by the lack of personnel and the war-time conditions in Sarajevo; that is to say that you were prevented from keeping an accurate list of any military targets by these factors?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we split it up? First, whether the witness agrees or not that there were limits in the possibilities to establish military targets. And then the second is what may have been the causes of -- if there are such limits. And then that was the question apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that as transcribed, the question says "very ability." And I think the question -- what you were saying, Mr. Ivetic, was "variability." So, sir, just so the witness understands the question probably, I think "variability," not "very ability."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we seek -- first of all, did you say "variability" or did you say the "very ability?"

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The very ability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very ability. So it's transcribed as you meant it. So the first part of the question or at least a simple question, Mr. Mole, were you limited in establishing what military targets may have been there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The section I'll address is the ability of the UNMO mission to identify or list conditions in Sarajevo. You, presumably, are making an assumption that the UNMO mission was in a vacuum but we were part of a sector that had three battalions. We had a sector headquarters, we had the UNMO mission, we had UNHCR, and many other agencies upon which we drew for our information. So, of course, with only 60 officers, I'm not suggesting that it was an easy task. But I think within the context of what I've just said our sources were somewhat greater than those that you give us credit for. Does that answer that part of that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So are you telling me then that you did have a complete and accurate list of all military targets in an area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This -- this seems to be a -- I'm addressing both you, Mr. Ivetic, and you, Mr. Mole. You are rather indirect in your questions. Mr. Ivetic asked you whether there were limitations in establishing the existence of military targets and to list them. And then apparently hearing in the question that -- and that's, of course, what Mr. Ivetic did, saying short of personnel, et cetera, to be the reasons, and then you start explaining that your sources may not have been as limited as suggested, although not expressed clearly by Mr. Ivetic. Now let me then try to put the question quite simply. Do you allow for the possibility that you may have missed military targets in your observations and on the basis of the information you had received? Or did you have a complete picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a fairly understandable picture. It wasn't recorded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me say, so it was not a complete picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's the simple thing we are establishing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, if I could say, your answer therefore is not complete but not too bad. That's more or less --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, if that's the question, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's the simple language we are using at this moment. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, Colonel, that especially the Bosnian Muslim Presidency side had a strong incentive to camouflage and keep hidden its military installations within Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both sides did that. But I agree with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you agree in so far as you have highlighted here the concern of the other side from finding out information from UNMO as to locations that the Bosnian Presidency forces had a strong incentive to keep some military sites unknown to the UNMO mission as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both sides would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to finish up, at paragraph 71 and 72 of this amalgamated statement you discuss the issue of military targets and the odd round, I believe, coming in. Would it be important to keep in mind the Bosnian Presidency forces tactic of using mobile mortars mounted on civilian vehicles which could be deployed essentially anywhere within the city which is not discussed in these paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You must always recall that in my statements I have made specific mention of those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we'll get to that later. Can we also agree that the artillery that we're talking about, the heavy weapons that were in use in and around Sarajevo on both sides of the conflict line were not the high-tech so-called smart artillery used by NATO allies in recent years but rather was the more inferior or average grade conventional weapons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the accuracy of such older generation artillery weapons as was available in the Sarajevo theatre is generally less than the newer generation artillery?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was well understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would that include a lesser degree of accuracy which would increase the potential for collateral damage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Based on your experience and knowledge within the British armed forces would you agree with me that the -- some NATO countries such as the United States have standard operating procedures to try and ensure there's no more than a 10 per cent chance of non-combatant injury, death or damage from any given military action?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put a figure on it, but your principle is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough. Could you tell us if you are familiar with the military term failed positive identification of a target and what that means.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't an artillery person myself. It's a term that I've never used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now for those who are unfamiliar with the terminology that you did use, can you briefly explain for us what is a range map or perhaps a firing table, if you're familiar with that term?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a acetate overlay onto a regular map. It would indicate ranges. It could indicate targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to Exhibit P3 on e-court, and it would be page 47 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, while we wait for this to come up, I will preface my comments by saying that this has been represented by the Prosecution to be a Sarajevo-Romanija Corps plan for artillery combat, the date of which, unfortunately, is not part of the document. Should be page 47 in e-court. It's page 41 in the book. There we go.
