Sir, looking at this map would this appear to be the type of a map that you had earlier indicated that you had seen in operations rooms on both -- on either side of the conflict line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: More so on the Serb side than the Presidency, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And does it appear to have information on it that you would expect to see for a map of this nature; that is, a plan for artillery combat.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really see much detail, but I understand your question, and, yes, I would expect at a distance that that would be the sort of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 49 which I believe is a close-up of some of the boxes that we cannot see precisely on this page. I think we'll see that this is titled as a firing table when we get to that page. And if we could rotate the -- oh, in the book -- I apologise, it's paragraph -- page 43 in the book. And, sir, if I can direct your attention to these two tables that appear to be for a 122-millimetre Howitzer and a 155-mm Howitzer, and is this the kind of information that you were discussing earlier about identified targets and ranges, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect that that sort of map, that sort of information, to be available to a commander inside an operations room. I can't say that I recall seeing such.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're looking at something now on the screen. I'm asking you about this one that's before us on the screen. Is that the kind of information that you would expect for an artillery fire mission to be available to a commander at which level I don't know, but at some -- at some level of the operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether these types of tables were available to your UNMO observers to assist in determining the outgoing shot's intended targets.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My UNMOs would only tell me information which they saw as pertinent. I don't recall ever seeing any of these tables. I don't recall ever speaking to an UNMO about such tables. My expectation would be that this would be in a headquarters rather than on a weapons site. But I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would it be your expectation that these targets would be identified by such means as observation, intelligence, et cetera, to locate and determine the co-ordinates, the dimensions, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this as a determination for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with me that if there is an error in the identification of targets before they are put on this table for whatever reason that that would cause considerable problems in terms of targeting by those artillery officers following such a table?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at all of the targets listed on this sample that we have before us and the dimension details for the same, would you agree that these are all apparently reasonable military targets?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the print is not quite big enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on the English version, perhaps that can assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The upper or the lower table?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's do the upper first. Maybe that might be easier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All those under target type dimension fulfil what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could look at the second table, the lower table. And, again, I'll ask you for the same comments, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that document. Thank you. If we can call up 65 ter 1D387. And while we wait for this, Colonel, I will give you the heads up that this is a statement which you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in 1997, and the first question I will have for you is, when it comes up, to look at the first page to confirm that in fact that is -- your signature is one of the signatures on this page?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn to the middle of the 13th page in the English version, which should amount to the bottom of page 11 in the B/C/S version. And, unfortunately, these paragraphs are not numbered, sir, but I would direct your attention to the selection that reads as follows: "My own feeling of the shelling by the Bosnian Serbs was that generally the local commanders did not take much notice of a range map. If they hit Sarajevo ... that was sufficient." First of all, sir, does this accurately reflect the position? And do you still hold that position that the local commanders were at fault for not using a range map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were incidents where what I have stated there are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're close to the time for a break. After the break, the first thing I'd like to do is to re-visit one of your previous questions, especially what it means if you ask whether these are reasonable military targets, because that is a rather unclear concept in this context. But we'll do that after the break. We'll take a break and resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, I said I would raise a matter after the break. You were asked, "Looking at all of the targets listed on this sample," and that was the previous document. It was P3. And I know that the hard copy --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 47 -- page 47 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 47 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 49 in e-court, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes: "Looking at all of the targets listed on the sample that we have before us and the dimension details for the same, would you agree that these are all apparently reasonable military targets?" Now, what did you understand to be a -- because you -- your answer was all those and the target type, dimensions fulfil what you said. What did you understand to be reasonable targets? Is that the dimensions fit the description or that using a Howitzer 155-millimetre would be a reasonable -- reasonably be used against these kind of targets? Whether the reasonability is depending whether a mortar is an urban area or somewhere outside. I had some difficulties in understanding exactly reasonable military targets are. And I'm also looking at it and sees that sometimes mortars get -- mortars and weapons, and whatever those weapons are, 100 by 100, I take it metres, whereas sometimes for weapons you get 100 by 100 but sometimes -- I'm looking at entry 4, for example, sometimes I see mortars, 200 by 100. What does it exactly mean? What did you agree to in relation to the question put to you by Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding was the target type was -- were they military targets, and I agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you would say a Howitzer is a -- could be -- reasonably would be a military target.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the same for weapons. But it doesn't say anything about the appropriateness of using the 150-millimetre Howitzer against these targets irrespective where they are situated. So it was just a Howitzer, seems to be a military target.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my interpretation, and, hence, my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear to me now. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For sake the continuity, if we can return to 1D387, page 13 in the English, and page 11 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Colonel, I believe before the break you had affirmed the quotation from your 1997 statement as still being accurate. If you could help us better understand this section that I read out, that you affirmed, to help us understand it better, would you premise -- would the premise behind this be that the problem wasn't in the orders that were being sent down but rather from the extralisation [sic] of the orders whether by lack of care or ineptness on the part of the local commanders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Your latter point could well be the case. My point throughout my testimony, however, relates to ammunition expenditure. And as a commander, I would wish to know how my ammunition was being used. So if we take your last point that a local commander wasn't accurate in terms of how much ammunition he fired, he exceeded, if there was limit, if he didn't have specific targets, I, as his commander, would want to know why he is doing what he is doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. I'd like to flush this out some more by walking through some of your testimony in the Karadzic proceedings with you. If we can call up now 1D00390 and it should be page 22 in the e-court. And this would be transcript page 5901 from that trial. And, sir, once this comes up, the question and answer that I would like to discuss is from lines 5 through 12 of the relevant page. And for the sake of being on the same page and allowing our B/C/S-speaking public to follow, the question was as follows: "Do you agree that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had inherited territorial and municipal armies that were already in existence, and everyone from General Sipcic to General Milosevic had great problems establishing a unified command structure over these local units? "A. It was certainly a significant difficulty which I observed that both sides had. This was not a unique experience from the Serb side. So I understand what you're saying. I was sympathetic to that situation, and I agree with your overall assessment." Do you affirm that this portion of your testimony that I've just quoted is accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that such a situation would have an effect upon understanding or explaining what we were discussing before, namely, that local commanders you felt were not paying attention to range maps and the shelling resulting therefrom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to the bottom portion of the page, line 19 and down further, and I apologise, but your answer will be on the next page, but if we can follow along. The question was -- and they're talking about a document: "Q. This is from the time of General Sipcic -- no, it was already General Galic. Colonel Marcetic writes here that the local leaders and their supporters are out of control in certain areas, and these difficulties are encountered all the time, starting with Sipcic who found the worse situation because it was early days. The VRS had just been set up. But even in November, the corps command is encountering the same problem. Is this consistent with what you confirmed earlier? " And, again, your answer is on the next page of the transcript: "A. Thank you. I've never seen the document, obviously, but it's fully in accord with what we understood to be the case. So, yes, I understand your point." Now do you affirm the accuracy and truthfulness of this portion of the trial record that I have read to you from the Karadzic proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you identify here that this situation was in full accord with what quote/unquote, "we understood the case to be." Who is the "we?" Are you referring to the UNMO mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, where did you get the "we?"

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is in your answer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, understood. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that such a situation would have an effect on understanding or explaining what we were discussing before, the local commanders that you felt were not paying attention to range maps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Moving along to another topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one follow-up question in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, you described here, or you agree to the description of inherited, not unified structures and the problems that caused. Now, what you saw happening on the ground, would that be mainly explained by these flaws or shortcomings? I mean, in terms of intensity of fire. Would you say, Well, this is what explains all this; or would you consider this to be a major part of the explanation, a minor part of the explanation? And if it does not fully explain, what would then additionally explain what you saw happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I answered the question as posed, which was, Was it contributory to. Yes, it was. Does it satisfy the observations that we made in terms of the quantity of munitions landing on Sarajevo? No, it doesn't. What I've always tried to do is to relate those rounds which we could not explain, not too forensically, because when anything up to 6- or 800 rounds are coming in on a day, it's not possible to do that. But what I'm stating is that as a commander, I would want to know why my subcommanders are firing and what they are firing at because munitions, like the other logistic elements, are a finite resource. So there is a responsibility upon the chain of command to know what is going on on the ground and why it's going on on the ground. The point that is being made relating to local commanders, of course, there will be an element of that. It's difficult to quantify because on one day you might get 200 rounds, on one day you might get 1600 rounds. I'm not going to put a percentage figure onto that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, one more question in relation to this. You said, I, as a commander would like to know how my ammunition was used. Would that also mean that a reasonable and responsible commander would improve the situation considerably if he would have noticed that mistakes as described were made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would expect the commander to impress upon his sub-commanders fire control. That really answers your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you see change over the time, where, of course, the inheritance in the beginning was, I would say an urgent one. It was -- did you see any such thing happen over time, as far as the accuracy of the firing was concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout my tour, which, in the overall period of the siege, is relatively small but intense in that three months, there wasn't a significant change within that period. But we tried to make a difference by approaching commanders and asking them to reduce fire if we didn't better receive that it was of a military -- with a military objective, and we were successful in that regard. So on a daily basis, we made a difference. But the difference that you're discussing relating to the proficiency of the services, we didn't notice a very significant change in the three months. But it is only a very small window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, as I was saying, I was ready to move on to another topic, the airport agreement. Would you agree with me that the so-called airport agreement which was actually entered into before your tour of duty to -- as -- as a SMO in Sector Sarajevo? While this agreement collected the heavy weapons that were in the possession of the Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Serb forces, it did not call or cause these weapons to be taken out of engagement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear that would mean that either side was free to utilise these heavy weapons from within the identified geographic areas covered by the agreement without being in violation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to return to 1D387, which again is the statement from 1997. And this time, if we can turn to the bottom of page 5 in the English and the middle of page five in the B/C/S. And it should be the last paragraph on this page that I am interested in and I will now read out for everyone: "The airport agreement of June 1992 was but a small step taken in the attempt to separate the factions in the city. This was a significant agreement to the Serb side as it gave up a considerable tactical advantage that it had won. By the same token, the decision and agreement to have UNMOs on heavy weapon sites on both sides was of greater significance to the Serbs than it ever was or could be to the weapon-light Presidency side. One must, therefore, appreciate that from the outset the Serbs being tactically in the ascendency were always the ones expected to give up more in any agreement. This certainly coloured their opinions and views in any negotiation on any topic. It was a common theme that I soon appreciated, but was not appreciated by others outside the UNMO group. The Serbs were, and still are, regarded as the perpetrators of the worse excesses, and their military advantage was always interpreted as demonstrating their aggression. While not defending their actions, there is a balance to be found."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, Colonel, could you stand by what you said in your statement and what I've read here now as being truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you can explain for us one aspect. Was it your understanding that the persons you identify as, quote/unquote, "others" in this selection, that they tended to lean on the Serbs harder than on the Bosnian Muslim Presidency side in terms of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you asking me to identify those persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not yet, no. I'm asking you if it was your understanding that these persons whom you have coined as others would lean on the Serb side harder in negotiations than on the Bosnian Presidency side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now are you able to better define others and I'm willing to take any qualifications, general terms. I leave it to you as to what you can give us in terms of a better idea of who these others would be.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think within UNPROFOR there was a general appreciation of the statement that you've just read out because they had first-hand experience of negotiations, and they, like the UNMO group, appreciated the overall situation. But I specify UNMO group there, because I'm not in a position to speak for other people. However, I personally had negotiations, discussions with others from my country, politicians, military people, who I don't want to name, but that was where, and I think in world terms, where the statement that I've made is true. And that was the balance that I was trying to redress.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I will not push you to name names. That answers --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- my question sufficiently. I'd now like to turn to a similar topic and the testimony from the Karadzic proceedings at 65 ter 1D389, and this will be page 78 in the e-court. And this, for the record, is transcript 5878 from the Karadzic proceedings. And the question starts at line 2 on this page, and I will again present to you the entirety of the question and answer and then ask for your comments: "And I see that, too, were very critical of the media and their reporting. I see in your amalgamated statement, paragraph 134, relates to the not-always-accurate reporting by the media. "MR. KARADZIC: [Interpretation] "Q. Do you confirm that? "A. Yes. I feel very strongly about the interpretation of events, as I saw them, from a position of comparative strengths. I think by virtue of the officers who worked for me, the knowledge I was able to gather, and the military and civilian interpretation that I applied was based on good evidence. I was always concerned that the evidence base that was used by certain agencies, and in this regard, I refer to news agencies, was extremely weak. I am, in my own mind, convinced that there was a considerable anti-Serb approach to the conflict within the press and, indeed, beyond it to some quite senior politicians who I met and talked with in Sarajevo." Can you confirm the truth and accuracy of the excerpt of your testimony as recorded in this transcript which I have now presented for you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with regard to the last part that the -- the persons coined as "quite senior politicians." First of all, I'm not going to ask you to name names. Are we talking about the same general group of people that was the answer to the previous question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you describe at least some of them as being persons with decision-making authority?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as far as the press is concerned, at paragraphs 133 through 134 of your amalgamated statement, which is P421, page 30 in the English and page 32 the B/C/S, you have already identified for us concerns about the reporting that you thought was unsubstantiated or anti-Serb, and you include a specific reference to the fabrication of a story by I believe it was BBC journalists. The question I have for you is to expand upon that. Did you have occasion to personally witness or have knowledge of journalists from other agencies that you could either identify or confirm being guilty of the same type of misdeeds, as these BBC journalists?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, it was one single individual. I had an excellent relationships with other elements of the same group, to the extent that I managed to place them in locations they would not otherwise have gone to, if it had not been for my inviting them to come with me. So this is about one specific journalist. In answer to your question about other journalists, I think I have mentioned in my testimony before I encouraged none of the UNMOs to discuss anything with the press, and if any discussion was to be had with the press, then it would be through myself. And I recall only ever speaking to the BBC. So, no, there were no other media agencies that I recall speaking to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And do you feel comfortable identifying for us the journalist whom you -- since we do have some that are coming to testify I'd like to make sure it is not one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps to be dealt with in private session. And also, if it would be a journalist still to appear, that he is not yet already aware of -- of the criticism. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to return for a moment back to the -- to something that you discussed in your prior testimony in the Karadzic. So this would be 1D390 in e-court and the relevant portion will be -- well, the answer is on page 3. Once we get that section up, perhaps ... I apologise. This should be -- can I see the page at the -- I'm sorry. It's the previous page - I apologise - page 2, I guess, it is in e-court. Should be at line 4. And the answer that you gave to a question that presented to you about complaints that General Morillon and Mr. Henneberry had about the media because of the biased positions that the media held and the same being hindrance for peace, your answer was as follows: "These opinions of which you speak which were held by the press, from our perception, certainly made it extremely more difficult for us to fulfil our mission, the details of which I'm sure you're aware, and will have made it difficult for the warring factions to proceed when their intentions, certainly from the Serb side, seemed to be warped and twisted by press reports." First of all, sir, do you stand by the selected portion of your testimony from the Karadzic case as being truthful and accurate, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I take it now here we are talking generally about press reports, not about specific journalists that you had encounters with. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, one follow-up question there. Did you follow the press reports of the whole of the world or the western world or Asia or Africa? What did you have access to and what were you able to read so as to form your opinion as expressed here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: European.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: European.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Put it simply, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: European means the whole of Europe including Russia, including --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, western European.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Western European.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you gain any impression about the reporting in -- even if not personally following it, were you ever receiving any reports about how the media were covering the situation, media you had no direct access to yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Because there were a mixture of battalions in Sarajevo, Egyptian, Ukrainian and French, one obviously picked up, not substantiated, but picked up the essence of what you are speaking about, how they were interpreting and at home, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: More specifically, Serbia, Russia, China, Indonesia, did you have any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Out of that list, Russia. I had been -- I think I've explained in sector east with a Russian battalion and of course then we had the Ukrainian battalion in Sarajevo. But, no, not to the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were they similarly distorting the good intentions of the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Russian element and the Ukrainian element were very much in favour of the Serb situation. I would therefore -- if I had to delineate it, say that the western media was generally the other way with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Colonel, could you expand for us on this understanding -- on your understanding of how this biased reporting, I guess, was making it difficult for you to fulfil your mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you consider the various tasks which we were trying to achieve there, I would want to focus, to answer your question, on the military elements, none of the others, because we were talking of hopefully a cease-fire, hopefully a disengagement. And once you start talking with the various sides about achieving that objective, and even going as far as trying to find local cease-fires to allow us to fulfil various utility missions, the response of -- from discussing these things with the warring factions they will have been affected by the issues of which we speak. And so as a consequence, they would come to the proceedings with a somewhat hardened attitude, a less forgiving one, and it would make negotiation that much harder to exercise. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have. Now I'd like to move a little bit beyond that. We talked about senior politicians and others in -- in a previous question. Do you feel that the approach or stance they had which I believe you described to be not understanding of the Serbs. Do you believe that that also affected the ability of negotiators to fulfil their mission in a same manner; that is to say, that it affected the parties and hardened their attitudes in negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Besides just one small correction which I would make, you -- you state, described to be not understanding of the Serbs. I would go further. I would say there wasn't a great comprehension of the complexities of the issues we were dealing with, not specifically Serbs. After that, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification and we can move on. Am I correct that with respect to Bosnian Muslim or Presidency forces, as far as they're concerned, when they utilised heavy weapons that were within the monitoring zone, that is, within the Papa side, the UNMOs would not necessarily have a clear indication of where that fire was directed. You could only present the statistical half picture if it landed somewhere near a Lima observer post in Serb territory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just let me read that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The numbers of heavy weapons on the Presidency side that we monitored was so small and the ammunition available to them so limited. I'll add a rider immediately. We didn't have all of them but those that we did have were seldom fired that I recall, so I can't answer your question relating to that because we were not monitoring the weapons they were using. Can I just give an example? There were three tanks. One fell off the road very quickly and was demobilised on the way to the airport. The other two I don't recall being used, because of the ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Can we focus on those weapons that you were not monitoring but which were being used, am I correct then that in that instance you would only have in terms of the statistics a record of where that shot landed potentially if it happened to land near a Lima position, because you did not obviously have the same coverage on the Lima side as you had on the Papa side. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if it was a -- I won't even use the term position because it could have been mobile, but if it was a site that was unmonitored you cannot exclude the possibility that it undershot or overshot a target and therefore landed on Papa territory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We wouldn't necessarily know where the fall-off shot was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up in e-court 65 ter number 1D393 for a continuation of this type of discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for the document I will let you know, sir, that this is an incident report for period 20 December 1992 to 21 December 1992 that bears your name at the bottom of the document. First of all, sir, having a chance to look at this one-page document can you confirm that you are familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the monitored weapons section in the upper half of the document, we see that the Bosnia Presidency positions are listed at number 2. For this period it is reflected that not a single shot was witnessed to be outgoing from the Presidency side. Am I correctly interpreting this part of the form?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at the increps which is at number 4, first of all, let's look at number 3. This records the amount of incoming rounds observed at the monitored sites of the Serb areas. And we see here a significant amount, that is, 16 artillery and 125 mortar shots incoming. Am I correct that this is precisely demonstrating what you have already told us that the Bosnian Muslim Presidency forces had artillery that was not monitored by your mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was talking previously I was being quite specific about within Sarajevo. This picture is the whole of that area, so it includes other locations beyond the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say "other locations beyond the city," would we include Mount Igman and Hrasnica as among other places as two points that were rather significant in terms of the artillery that was available to the Presidency forces which was outside of Sarajevo, outside of the Papa side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And remembering that artillery is a mobile function.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. If I could just return to this document for a moment. So we are clear, do you permit the possibility that the incoming rounds suffered by the Serb-controlled areas could actually be in excess of what is reflected on this form, again because of the lack of the coverage of the entirety of the Serb-controlled areas by the UNMO mission which was mainly monitoring weapons on that side of the line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with regard now moving to the Mount Igman location in particular, am I correct that you were persistent but unsuccessful in trying to place observers at Igman, at the Presidency positions there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that a significant factor relating to discrepancies in the various reports of this nature would be due to the fact that UNMO had no insight as to the outgoing fire from Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did actually have some insight. Because within my statements - I can't recall exactly where - a UN military observer did go up onto Mount Igman and he did count the weapons, which I can't recall instantly that I stated at the time. So with a snap-shot of this particular event, it gives you an indication of the weapons available to the Presidency side on Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I promise you I will not ask you for instant recall for those figures. I do know that I have them somewhere in my questions so we will get to them, and I will be fair enough to provide you the relevant portion of your statement so we do not have to guess. But for the time being, with respect to Mount Igman itself, would you agree that this was a significant geographical feature and also a feature of military significance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And focussing now on the time of your tour in Sarajevo, the three months that you were there, am I correct that this location, this feature, was held by the Presidency forces throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall if this feature had a residential nature to it or was it purely military, Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never went there, so I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Would Mount Igman and the forces situated there have had an unobstructed view of the entirety of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine so from the geographical layout, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as such, would these forces have the ability to target any of the Serb or Presidency-held areas of the city itself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dependant on the type of weapon that they had there at any one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the range --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ranges that the weapon; hence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the Lima or Serb artillery shooting at the BiH forces on Igman would be recorded as outgoing but would not be recorded on the forms as incoming, in so far as there were no observers near Igman?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And likewise, outgoing fire from Igman that overshot targets or undershot targets that could potentially land on Presidency-held territory, it, too, would not be identifiable as coming from Igman, if you can understand that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you mean. But since we don't know what was there and whether it was the source of the fire, we're only looking at an impact and, of course, that could have come from anywhere. But I do understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me simply it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that the monitors on the Papa side recording incoming shot would not be able to distinguish between fire that potentially came from Igman or potentially came from both monitored and unmonitored Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me that it was not only likely but in fact a certainty that the Serb artillery was targeting Igman and either engaging in offensive or counter-offensive fire with the forces on Igman?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would such fire, whether offensive or defensive counter-fire be military justified or legitimate, in your opinion or estimation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems to be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to all the reports and the various incident forms that we have discussed or that you discussed in your statement and testimony, am I correct that we should keep in mind that the number of outgoing shoots -- shots from the Serb artillery included or could include shot that was directed at Igman rather than upon the Papa side or the Papa zone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And from this document, at least for this time-period, the Serb positions suffered more incoming shot directed at them than did the Papa or Presidency side have incoming shot directed at them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at items 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would ask for this document that's on the screen to be tendered into evidence and given the next available exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is 1D393?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number D83, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Ivetic. Would this be a suitable time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break, and we resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, as promised, I have located the portion of your statement dealing with the recon of the Igman location. If we can call up in e-court in 1D387 and this will be pages 11 in the English and 10 in the B/C/S. And while we wait for that, sir, I would like to see if I can verify something else with you. In respect of the Presidency forces that would have been located at the Mount Igman location, would you agree that there was both infantry and artillery at this location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And if we look at bottom of the page in English that we have before us of 1D387, and I will read out for you the selection so that hopefully you can locate the same: "I was later able to substantiate by way of a rec conducted by two of my UNMOs that the Presidency forces on Igman had two times APCs; one time 130-millimetre Howitzer; four times 105-millimetre field guns; two times 122-millimetre field guns; and six times 120-millimetre mortars." Does this accurately and truthfully represent the recon information you had about the artillery available to the Presidency forces at the Mount Igman location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the memory I had, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you also recall of receiving constant complaints from the Serb side that precisely these Presidency forces on the Mount Igman location were conducting fire upon civilian areas in the Serb-held portions of Sarajevo, particularly the Ilidza suburb?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we received complaints on many occasions, and I think they are recorded in my statement for General Galic, as it is stated in my statement from General Galic that he threatened to return fire on Sarajevo if it continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you previously talked about the Bosnian Presidency forces within the Papa zone, that is to say, within the inner parts of the city, as having lack or minimal ammunition. Would you agree with me that the forces at the Mount Igman location were not subject to the same difficulties in resupply that the forces in the Papa zone had?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Am I correct that in addition to the Mount Igman location the Bosnian Presidency forces held several other points of high ground outside of the city where forces and heavy weapons were located?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other locations that heavy weapons could be brought to bear from the Presidency, yes. My personal experience of them though is not. I have none.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Would you agree with me that we cannot view the UNMO statistics as an exact representation of the fire from Serb artillery into the city, but rather that it can be only viewed as an inexact attempt to indicate levels of activity rather than assess where all shots came from or went?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever we could, we would make a relationship between outgoing fire from the Lima side to incoming fire on the Presidency side, and as we've seen, there are variations which are not explained by the pure statistics. So, yes, it was not an exact science, something I've said I think a number of times in my various statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I was about to say that the witness has explained this various times, but he himself did it as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If I could call up in e-court number 1D00394.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for the document, sir, I'd like to advise you that it is dated the 10th of December, 1992, and appears to be a report authored by Lieutenant Commander Rees on your behalf send to the CMO UNPROFOR in Zagreb. Can you verify for us or recognise this document as being one that was prepared or on your bequest or with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've signed it so that is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the section entitled "general situation," we see that it states for the period 9 to 10 December 1992 the following: "Medium to low level of activity today with 35 rounds incoming to Presidency side and 91 rounds incoming to Serb side. Total rounds recorded outgoing from Serb positions 189, from Presidency positions," I believe it's a 50 or a 53, I can't tell, "and shelling widely dispersed throughout the city." Would you agree with me that on this date, too, the Serb positions were enduring three times more incoming shots than the Presidency positions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic that is now the second time that you apparently think that what is reported here that the Chamber is unable to establish that the 189 is three times approximately 50 or 53. Earlier you asked the witness whether the one had more incoming fire than the other side. This Chamber, perhaps not good in mathematics, but these basics are really within our -- within our competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, these are public proceedings and the Office of the Prosecutor has been allowed to present a summary of the witness's testimony, which is for the public's information, and we believe that material that contradicts that or provides more information and a more complete picture -- for the public to know the full aspects of this witness's available testimony and of the circumstances in Sarajevo during the relevant time-period are necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm not blaming you for reading that there were 35 rounds incoming and, et cetera, I'm not blaming you for mentioning it. But then to say whether 150 is three times 50, that, of course, is in addition to putting the figures and is really totally unnecessary. That's what my point is. Not -- and I didn't blame you for pointing at the numbers. I blamed you for the question that you put to the witness which seems to assume that the Chamber is -- and the public is unable to establish that 189 is more than three times 50 or 53. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the bulk of the incoming fire or -- strike that. Would you suspect that some of the incoming fire on the Serb positions would be precisely from unmonitored BiH Presidency artillery or heavy weapons whether on Mount Igman or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figures suggest that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you consider it reasonable or likely that the Serb positions, if taking incoming fire from these Presidency positions, would fire outward towards these BiH Presidency positions to counter or neutralise the threat?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a reasonable expectation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would such outgoing fire be militarily justified?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the premise of the target, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that this document be admitted into evidence with the next available Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D387 becomes Exhibit D84, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 387 or 394?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think it's 394.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 394, your correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So Exhibit 1D394 received D84, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could take a look at 1D392 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, again while we're waiting for the document I can advise that you it is dated the 19th of November, 1992, and appears to have been prepared by Major Rosenroll, and perhaps can you verify if it in fact has been signed by you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the time-period covered by 18 to 19 November 1992, we see that under item 1 with the low to medium activity only one shot fell in Presidency territory whereas 16 shots fell onto Serb territory. And here you explain that the Serbs were firing 57 rounds although only one landed on the territory of the Presidency forces that you monitored.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I highlight that clearly, I think, the limitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree that this document and your explanation contained therein perhaps most drastically explains the point we were discussing previously as to the limitations as to these statistics?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I've explained in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here there appears to have been a cease-fire that has failed. Do you recall based upon the fact that the Zuc and Nedzarici locations are mentioned, and the fact that only one shot was incoming to the BiH side if this was a cease-fire that the Presidency forces would have broken?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't make a judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document into evidence as the next available Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D392 becomes Exhibit D85, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, on the topic of cease-fires at paragraph 29 of your amalgamated statement, Exhibit P241, and it would be the eighth page in English and the sixth page in the B/C/S, at this paragraph once it comes up - I'll wait for that - I would direct your attention to the conclusory statement at the end of this paragraph, which starts as follows: "Throughout my tenure, the level of activity always exceeded our ability to respond to every incident as there was never an effective cease-fire." Would you agree with me that all parties to the conflict in Sarajevo were responsible for such a situation that they all violated cease-fires at various times?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can only violate a cease-fire if you have one. I don't recall one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, generally speaking, that the Presidency side was more reluctant to enter into a general or universal cease-fire in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thinking back to the negotiations that I was party to, both on an individual basis and with the individuals who I worked closely with on both sides, and at the mixed military working group, I don't recall that they were any more likely to object to a cease-fire. I sensed that their position meant that they would welcome it by virtue of the weight of weaponry that was ranged against them. But, no, I don't think there was any greater emphasis on the Presidency side, working from memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Then can I move on to the issue of utilities. At paragraphs 10 and 11 of your amalgamated statement - that would be 3 and 4 in the English - you identify utility works and repairs as an item that the UNMO mission was tasked with. I'd like to focus up -- focus on that for a moment, but, first, I'd like to present to you what another witness, Mr. Pyers Tucker, testified to in the Galic case and which he affirmed here a few weeks ago. So if we can please have 1D367 up on the screen, and this is the transcript pages 10029 to 10031 from the Galic case beginning at line 12. To be fair, I will provide you the entirety of the exchange before asking you to comment on particular items: "Q. The last question is you have told us about one of the tasks performed was to discuss issues of restoring utilities: Gas, water supply, electricity. Could you tell us whether the parties were co-operative if it came to restoring these utilities, whether both parties behaved similarly or differently? Could you elaborate a bit more on that? "A. Utilities were something which General Morillon considered very important, and at the meetings at which utility repair was discussed, both sides were entirely co-operative. These meetings were very complex because you needed to bring to one place, at one time, both technicians who had the right knowledge and a cease-fire that was agreed by both sides, and the technicians needed to know a safe route through the minefields in order to reach the area that they needed to carry out repairs. "When we looked at what happened on the ground, the co-operation," and now we have to go to the next page of the transcript, "the co-operation which we received from the Bosnian Serb authorities was generally of a high order. The co-operation we received from the Bosniak local commanders varied considerably, and it was our belief that in some areas where the Presidency authorities had high control, things generally went well. But there were other areas where the local commanders were radical, and from the perspective of general discipline and obedience, were unreliable, that all sorts of tricks were used in order to prevent the repairs from taking place. "JUDGE ORIE: I'm trying to understand this. The supplies of water, electricity and gas also served their own population. What was the specific reason why they would play tricks which would result in not restoring the supplies when their own population would suffer from it? Do you have any explanation about that? "A. I do have an explanation and it is as follows: There were elements within the Bosnian leadership who believed that the only way to take back that which had been taken from them by the Bosnian Serbs, that could only happen by either international intervention in Bosnia or by the provision of arms and ammunition to Bosnia which was not possible at that time because of the arms embargo. Those people believed that the only way to secure such international assistance was to depict the situation in Sarajevo to be so severe that the international community would be -- would be willing to intervene. Therefore, it was not in their interest to see any improvement in the situation in Sarajevo. It was not in their interest to see any -- to see the lot of the civilian population improve. To put it bluntly, the more suffering, the better, because that...," and if we turn to the last page for the last two lines, "... because that played to the television cameras and would ultimately lead to the pressure that they wanted in order to achieve international intervention." Now, I'd like to first ask you about the first part of Mr. Tucker's testimony regarding the difficulties of negotiating joint repair missions to the utilities. Does that accord with your recollection of the situation and, indeed, that at least some sort of local cease-fire was necessary to effectuate these missions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we return to that page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That would be the first page, page 1 in e-court. And, by all means, there's something that has been omitted by Mr. Tucker as to difficulties, you could add to that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It such a lengthy element of the document that there are so many issues in there, it's almost difficult to know where to start. Are you going to specifically ask me a question about a specific part of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about the specific part from lines 18 to 24 on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does that comport with your recollection of the difficulties of getting repair missions to the utilities during the time-period when you were at Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I give a little background before I answer your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Briefly, yes --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because it is very pertinent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- if you can, if you can.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. General Morillon was BiH commander. Major Tucker worked for him, a British officer whom I knew very well. General Morillon and Major Tucker would know as much about the utility missions as they gleaned from the various situation reports that I wrote. Before I went to Sarajevo, there were no utility missions. I instigated them. I ran every single one. It is therefore quite difficult for me to read what somebody else thinks about them when actually they had no direct contact with the utility missions whatsoever. So within the lengthy paragraph, there are elements which are true, but there are also areas where there is confusion. The meetings were complex, yes, I did them. They took many days to ensure that by virtue of their location, more often than not on the front line, both sides knew what was happening, where it was happening, and, indeed, the technicians that we required to fulfil that mission. To achieve it, I did considerable amount of negotiating myself, and I had a particular officer who looked after most missions, and he also did negotiations. Therefore, it was right down the chain of command, from General Galic on the one side, to Mr. Siber on the other side, right down to local commanders. Where some of these failed, I wouldn't put a figure on as to whether it was one side, nor the other. Because the important point from my perspective was that if it wasn't safe for the technicians and the UN -- UNPROFOR people who were there, then I wouldn't do it. Earlier on in the day, we talked about blame one way or the other. I wasn't interested in blame, and I worry a little that this document and this statement seems to give an emphasise more on one side than the other. For every single mission that we sent out, and I think eventually we had a success rate of about 65 per cent, which in the circumstances was phenomenally successful, it indicates that actually there was a willingness on both sides to achieve what we were trying to achieve. But this was war. Elsewhere in my statements I recall clearly stating that I think I said the water didn't come on one side so they shelled the electricity substation --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that was typical. So I think those first few lines there are elements of truth about it, but I think my explanation is slightly more accurate, and so it should be. I ran them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's why I asked you. And did you share the view of Mr. Tucker that at times it appeared that segments of the Bosnian Presidency leadership or perhaps local commanders seemed to be reluctant to assist in the utilities due to their desire to obtain either intervention or to effectuate an end to the arms embargo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's mixing up too many features. We had difficulty completing utility missions from both sides, for multiple reasons. It wasn't our task to analyse why it failed. What we did do was try to learn so that if we could manage the same utility mission another time, or something similar, then we would have learnt from that experience. We didn't go as far as analysing it. Can I say where I think the failures really occurred? And it was common wherever we did these missions. And it was on the local basis. That is very true and that is the common feature through -- that I have with this particular statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And now I can leave that document and go to 1D391, which, while we wait for it, sir, is again a report that emanated from your mission, I believe; albeit in a different format. It appears to be dated the 17th of October, 1992. Can you take a look at this and at least from the first page can you tell whether this is something that would have emanated from your position, from your office? If you like, we can also go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, did you say 17th of September? Because that is dated the 4th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought it was 17th of October, but I could be ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. 17th of October. Sorry. I thought you said September which would be the day after I arrived. So, yes, I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, you're with me. Now, does this appear to be a message or report that would have been -- emanated from your position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from SMO Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, first, if we look at item 1 since it's up on the screen, we -- we see that the statistics demonstrate that more shot was falling on to the Serb-controlled territories than was falling on the Presidency-controlled territories, at least for this period covered by this sitrep. Would you agree with me - now that we've gone through several of these reports - that there were times when the incoming fire was heavier against the Serbs than against the city parts controlled by the Presidency forces, even though I don't think that that was identified in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You just have to look at the figures for that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to focus on the part of the document that is entitled "continuous affairs." We have to scroll down just a little bit. The middle of the page. Right there is fine. And here precisely you are discussing problems with local commanders in terms of -- on both sides actually, with respect to some three utility missions that were planned for the day. Is that -- is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does this accurately memorialise some of the general items that you had just testified about? Does this give a specific indication of a particular instance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it clearly relates to those three utility missions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would at this time tender this document as the next available Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't have necessarily an objection to this but just as to the date. I think counsel is referring on top to a date that's printed on the top there. I'm not sure that that 17 October date is the actual date of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I can assist the parties. The language used at the top line is "afgedrukt" on the 17th, which means printed on the 17th. Then, yes, if we agree all on that, that it's just the date of the print.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D391 becomes Exhibit D86, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, we have only three minutes left. I would like to already excuse the witness for the day and continue tomorrow, and I would like to address one or two issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, we'll adjourn for the day, soon. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, and I again instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with any other person about your testimony irrespective of whether already given or still to be given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Time is too limited. But, Mr. Ivetic, there are a few documents you have used and not tendered, you may have intentionally done so, a lot was read into the record, but please be aware there are four documents of that kind. Then, second, I earlier said something about that the Chamber is able to make its own math. But then, unfortunately, I took the wrong portion, because your question was about the incoming fire, so your question was about whether 91 is three times 35, and now not that that is a more complex calculation than the one I mentioned, because the Chamber is able both to establish that 91 is -- and that's the incoming fire on the Serb side, was three times what was incoming on the Presidency side, and the Chamber was also able to calculate that the outgoing fire from the Serb side, 189, was more than three times the outgoing fire from the Presidency side. But that's hereby corrected. The other matter I'd like to briefly raise is scheduling. Could you tell us approximately how much time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I anticipate another hour, 15; hour, 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As matters stand at this moment, Ms. Hochhauser, could you give an indication as to how much you think you would need in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: As matters stand at this moment, I have about four questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which means that the next witness scheduled tomorrow that we'll easily conclude his examination-in-chief tomorrow somewhere during the second session most likely. I wondered to what extent it would be possible to condense the cross-examination of the next witness in such a way that he could be excused before the weekend. Would you seriously consider that and see to what extent that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it the next witness after this one, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, he is scheduled for half an hour, as I understand it, and for -- I think you scheduled him for three hours. Now if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Two and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two and a half hours, which makes all together three hours. We have -- I'm not saying that you should, but if it would be possible to -- to accommodate the witness by -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are a bit unclear at this moment, Your Honour, because we just learned during the last break that that witness is coming tomorrow, so we are not clear yet how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there may be some confusion. The witness has no protective measures so it's the witness Elvir Pasic who has been on the schedule for some time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He is scheduled for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, I think that's the witness. I know Mr. Lukic has been dealing with the matter of the Detention Unit. Perhaps I can speak with him at the break and clarify some of the recent developments with respect to the witness that we had considered moving forward but ultimately did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But as matters stand now, we expect the next witness to be called to be Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we're wondering whether there be -- whether it would be possible by both parties using the time in the most -- in the most efficient way, whether we could achieve that the witness could be excused before the weekend. If not, of course, we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you are aware by now that we do our best to comply with your orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, well, first of all, this was not an order, but I think we -- we share our concern about the well-being and how to best to accommodate witnesses and that's -- the Chamber appreciates that both parties are always very much attentive to that. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 2nd of November, at 9.30 in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 2nd day of November, 2012, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.18 p.m.,
